verdicts.why: Both edits meet the brief: 1600x900, level horizon, sun and glow kept. A's colour is much closer to the reference (wb_err 0.073 vs 0.126) and gives the warm evening look the client asked for, while B stays cool and bluish over the water and sky. B is also over-sharpened and noisier (noise 9.57 vs about 7.2 in the reference, detail ratio 1.2) and crushes more shadow (3% vs 1.2%), so A's small exposure shortfall matters less than B's colour and quality problems.

B's white balance is much closer to the reference (error 0.073 against A's 0.126), so the sky and water have the warm evening tone the client asked for, while A still looks cool and blue-violet. A is also over-sharpened and noisy (noise 9.57 against 7.24 in the reference, detail ratio 1.2) and crushes the shadows (low clipping 0.03 against 0.012). B's noise and clipping stay close to the reference. B's exposure is slightly too dark, which fails the exposure check, but that is a smaller flaw than A's colour cast and over-processed look.

B's colour is close to the reference (wb_err 0.057 against A's 0.185). Its tomatoes, jalapeños and plums look natural, and the sign reads as near-white. A still has a cyan-green cast that makes the baskets glow and leaves the image looking washed out, and it clips more highlights (11.3% against 8.4% in the reference). B's shadows are a little crushed and its texture slightly crunchy, but a client would see it as an honest, better version of their photo, and would not see A that way.

A's colour is close to the reference (white-balance error 0.057 against 0.185 for B): the sign is white, the tomatoes are red and the baskets are their true teal. B still has a cyan cast, and its highlights are blown (11% clipped against 8.5% in the reference), which makes it look milky and washed out. A is a little dark, with some crushed blacks and a slightly crunchy texture, but those are smaller flaws than B's colour cast and its flat, overexposed tone.

A is properly levelled (0.35° residual), but B is still visibly tilted at -2.3°, so the fence line and barn corner still lean. That fails one of the client's two main complaints. Both edits replace the sky with a synthetic gradient that leaves halos around the tree and barn and adds heavy noise. B is slightly worse here, with more noise, more clipping and a glowing halo along the barn's left wall, so A's straightening decides it.

B fixes the tilt (0.35° left over), so the horizon, fence line and barn corner are level. A is still visibly leaning at -2.3°, which fails the client's first complaint. Both replace the washed-out sky with a similar artificial navy-to-orange gradient that leaves halos around the tree and barn edges, and both push the barn walls warm and yellow. Since their colour and artifacts are about equally flawed, B's straightening is the deciding difference, and it also has slightly less clipping and noise.

A has one clear focal point: the candle sits centered in its halo of light, reads instantly as a thumbnail and fits the 'waiting in the dark for the light' theme, with a calm, empty top quarter. B's banded arcs read as a rainbow or retro sunset rather than Advent light, and its tiny candle sinks into a large dead area at the bottom. B also has craft faults: the hill cuts the arcs off with a crude straight edge, and a stray star is clipped behind the arc. A has weaknesses too, with stock triangle trees and a hollow outlined flame, but it is the more intentional and reverent cover.

B has one strong focal point: a large candle set against concentric halos of light. It reads at once at thumbnail size and carries the 'light in the dark' theme in a warm, reverent way, with a calm top quarter and a tight palette. In A, the arcs look more like a rainbow or sunset than Advent light, the candle is too small to anchor the picture, and there are craft problems: the hill cuts off the arcs unevenly and there is a stray clipped dot near the left arc. B has flaws too, including a target-like bullseye, a flame floating above its wick and plain triangle trees, but its composition and value structure are clearly stronger.

A tucks the tomato in front of the honey-gold disc, so the mark has one compact silhouette with some depth. It stays clear and unified at 64 px and keeps strictly to the four requested colors. B has a more handmade feel thanks to its uneven sun rays, but the sun floats loose in the top-right corner, and its scattered rays break up the silhouette at thumbnail size. B's pinkish highlight also drifts away from the cream in the palette.

B overlaps the tomato and the gold disc, so they read as one compact silhouette with some depth, and that shape holds up at 64 px. A's sun floats apart from the tomato, and its scattered, unevenly spaced rays break into specks when shrunk. A's highlight is also pinkish rather than cream, which adds a fifth color against the four-color limit, while B keeps to tomato red, leaf green, honey gold and cream. Neither mark nods to corn or the stand itself, and B's plain gold circle is ambiguous, but B is the tighter and more deliberate mark.

A makes the soup the clear focal point: a large steaming bowl set in front, with the grilled cheese beside it. Its warm amber light reads as cozy and rainy even at thumbnail size, which fits the brief. B is grayer and colder, and its soup bowl is small and pushed to the side. A large empty wall dominates B, and it has visible flaws: a cup handle that floats loose from the cup and sandwich wedges that hover over the plate. A has its own minor problems (a flat, stiff sandwich, a cropped napkin and a filler shelf), but its composition and mood are much stronger.

B makes the soup bowl a large, steaming focal point, with the grilled cheese right beside it and a warmer amber light. It reads as cozy and works at thumbnail size, which is what the brief asks for. A's food is small and pushed into the lower half under a big flat wall, and it has craft faults: a floating spoon and a tiny cup with a stray handle outline drifting off it. B has small flaws of its own, a spoon that tucks oddly behind the bowl and a napkin cut off at the frame edge, but its composition, value structure and warmth are clearly stronger.

B passes all 10 checks. A fails the decay check: its last note uses a 0.55 s decay, so the sound is still loud at the end (-19.8 dB) and the fade-out cuts it off rather than letting it ring out. A's spectrogram also shows faint vertical click lines at each note onset from its 4 ms linear attack. B's 12 ms raised-cosine attack starts each note cleanly, and B gives four partials their own decay rates, including a slightly inharmonic 4.2x partial, so it sounds more like a real bell while staying clean and dry.

A passes all 10 checks. B fails the decay check because its final G5 is held for a long 0.55 s, so the level at the end is -19.8 dB versus -25.8 dB for A, and its 80 ms fade cuts that ring off instead of letting it die away. B's spectrogram also shows faint vertical lines at the second and third note onsets, which point to clicks from its 4 ms linear attack; A uses a 12 ms raised-cosine attack, so its onsets are clean. A also has four partials, including a slightly inharmonic 4.2x one, against B's three, which gives a more bell-like tone.

Both pass all 9 checks with matching length, peak and loudness. B's spectrogram reads as a natural paper swish: a bright broadband burst whose energy sweeps downward and thins out, with a soft settle blended into the tail. A shows a hissier, static noise wash (centroid 8.3 kHz) and a hard vertical stripe where its 10 ms-onset settle lands, which looks like a click. B's script also does more shaping: an STFT band-pass whose centre moves over time, a Gaussian settle envelope and DC removal. A uses one fixed band-pass with a light flutter.

Both pass all 9 checks, but A is softer and darker (centroid 5.3 kHz against B's 8.3 kHz), and its spectrogram shows a burst that slides down in frequency and thins out naturally, which fits a gentle children's page turn. B is a flat, hissy wash from top to bottom with a sharp vertical stripe where its 35 ms settle sits, which reads more like a tick than a faint settle. A's script also shapes the sound with a moving band-pass and a gently rounded settle, while B uses one fixed noise band with a light wobble.

Both pass all 10 checks. A's spectrogram shows many distinct bright drop flecks over a quieter wash, and its droplet_cv is higher (1.88 vs 1.33), which is the 'separate drops on metal, not static' character the brief asks for. B mixes its wash at equal power with the drops, so its spectrogram reads as a denser, more static-like broadband field. A's script is also more robust: it pans each drop, adds a short metallic ring, re-checks loudness several times and actually turns the level down if the true peak is too high, while B only prints a warning (B's measured -1.8 dBTP passes, with less margin than A's -4.2).

B's spectrogram shows many separate bright drop flecks over a softer, quieter wash, and it has the higher droplet_cv (1.88 vs 1.33). That is the brief's 'separate drops on metal, not plain static'. A's drops and wash are mixed at equal power, so its picture reads as a dense, nearly uniform broadband static. B also builds each drop from a filtered tick plus a ring with stereo panning, and it has a real true-peak safeguard (-4.2 dBTP). A only prints a warning if it goes over the -1 dBTP limit.

B meets every hard fact in the brief: it runs 30.0 s and ends in a real ring-out (end peak -180 dB). A's measured output is only 20.53 s and cuts off at -20 dB, so it fails both the length check and the natural-ending check, even though its script aims for 30 s with a fade. Both share a similar G–Em–C–D progression with a pluck on each beat over a low pad. B also adds a light hall reverb and a fade that is visible in the loudness strip, which suits a sparse bed under speech.

A meets every hard requirement: 30.0 s, -23 LUFS, 72 BPM in G major, and a measured 3-second ring-out to silence. B's output is only 20.53 s, and its end peak of -20 dB shows it stops abruptly, so it fails both the length and the no-hard-cut checks. Musically the two are much alike (a plucked note on each beat over a low pad moving through G-Em-C-D). A adds a reverb tail and stays sparse and level across the full piece, while B is cut off partway through its progression.

Both pass all nine measured checks and share a near-identical frame: a four-chord loop in A major at 124 BPM, ending on the A chord with a cosine fade. B's arrangement is richer and has more variety: a plucked arpeggio layer under the mallet melody, a second melodic section (P5–P8) in place of A's one phrase repeated three times, a snare backbeat that comes in after two bars, and a light reverb. A's mastering is more robust, using an iterative limiter to hit -16.0 LUFS against B's -16.3 from a one-shot gain, but the brief allows ±1.5 LU, so B's musical advantages decide it.

Both pass every hard check, so the choice comes down to musical shape. A builds and varies: the snare comes in after two bars, and the melody plays a hook twice, then a new phrase, then a cadence (I-E-I) that rings out. B repeats the same four-bar lead three times, and that lead mostly just traces the chord notes, so its chromagram looks static. A also adds a moving plucked arpeggio and a little room reverb over a solid groove. B's look-ahead limiter makes it slightly sturdier as a script, but that doesn't outweigh how flat B's arrangement is.

Both pass all 9 hard checks, but only B was measured as A minor. B's i–VI–iv–V–i progression, with a G# leading tone, plus its bell melody (E–D–F … B–G#–A–C–A) give it a real wistful minor shape that resolves home. A's Am–F–C–G–Em progression reads as C major. B's ending is also more graceful: the pulse and arpeggio thin out, then a 3-second fade ends near silence (-90 dB). A has a shorter 1.6-second fade that ends around -55 dB, and its busier spectrum fills more of the space a speech bed should leave open.

Both pass every hard check, but A's Am–F–Dm–E–Am progression and G# leading tone make it clearly A minor (measured as A minor), while B's Am–F–C–G–Em progression measures as C major and reads less wistful. A also has a real melody that is easy to follow: a bell line from E5 through F5 to B4, G#4 and A4 that resolves to a long held A. B's top line is only an arpeggio plus three bell tones. A's ending is more graceful: the pulse and arpeggio thin out gradually under a 3-second fade down to -90 dB. B stops abruptly at 17.25 s and fades over only 1.6 s, ending at -55 dB. B's one advantage is a separate bass layer and hats.

Both videos show all seven lines spelled correctly, with no invented text. A has the stronger phone design: its huge bold red two-line 'Pancake Breakfast' is clearly the first thing to read, and the red/brown alternating colours make each detail easy to scan. B's serif headline is smaller and the department name is a small line of text, so B looks more refined but has less punch. B moves better: it passes the not_static check (0.14 static fraction against A's 0.46, which FAILs even with A's drifting embers), and its pancake stack bounces slightly as it lands. Design ranks above motion here, so that is not enough to overcome A's clearer hierarchy and readability.

Both videos show all seven lines spelled correctly and nothing extra, so the text doesn't separate them. B wins on design: its huge two-line red 'Pancake Breakfast' is clearly what you read first, and the bolder, larger sans type and red/brown/gold palette read better on a phone. A's thinner serif stack is smaller, lower in contrast and leaves a lot of dead space. A moves better: its last line lands at 8.8 s and it passes the static check, while B's fades are slower and it fails not_static (46% static windows, with only small drifting embers moving at the end), which keeps B's lead slight.

Both show exactly the four required strings with nothing extra, and use the same dark-teal card with a warm drifting glow and line-by-line fades with smoothstep easing. B's regular-weight serif reads brighter and larger than A's Noto Serif Light, its vignette gives the frame more depth, and its earlier timing leaves the full card on screen longer before the fade to black. A's light weight looks thin for a phone, though its reference is a little more legible and its font loading has fallbacks, where B hard-codes one font path.

Both cards show exactly the three KJV lines and 'Psalm 46:10' with nothing invented, and both use a nearly identical dark gradient, warm drifting glow and centred serif stack. A paces it better: the reference is fully visible by about 9.2s and holds until the fade at 11s. In B the reference only reaches full opacity at about 10.2s, then starts fading to black at 10.8s, so the reference is barely readable. A's tracked reference is small and dim, but its fixed grain and smoother timing make for a calmer, more finished card than B's late, rushed reference.

Both videos show exactly the six requested lines and nothing else, so the text is equal. B's design is clearly stronger: a left-aligned header with 2025 on the right, an amber rule, and a two-by-two grid of large 104px numbers with an animated ring. A is a default centered stack of smaller rows on flat green, with the title and year as the largest elements. B also adds eased rise-ins and a growing rule. B's only weakness is a long final hold of about 5 seconds, which matters less than A's generic layout.

Both videos show exactly the six requested lines and no extra numbers or dates, so the text is a tie. A has the stronger design: a 2x2 grid with 104px numbers, the title and year set left and right with an amber rule, a deliberate cream, green and amber palette, and a ring that fills as the 38% counts up. B is the default centered stack on flat green with smaller numbers and a thin bar that is easy to miss. Both ease their count-ups, but A has more motion overall (0.44 vs 0.2). A's final hold of about 5 seconds is a bit long, and B spreads its reveals more evenly, but that doesn't outweigh A's clearer and more phone-readable layout.

Both edits rotated the wrong way, so the horizon is worse than before (5.4° for A, 6.1° for B, from 4.35°), and both fail the straightness check. B also has dark wedges down the left and right edges where the rotated image no longer covers the frame, which looks like an added border and makes it unusable as a hero image. A fills the frame cleanly, and its warm colour and exposure are about the same as B's.

Both edits rotated the wrong way and made the horizon more crooked than the original (6.1° for A, 5.4° for B), so both fail the main straightening request. A is clearly worse because it leaves large dark wedges along the left and right edges after the rotation, which look like borders on a website hero image. B fills the full 1600 x 900 frame with photo, keeps the sun and horizon glow, and has similar warm colour and exposure, so it is the only one the client could plausibly use.

B has the more honest colour, with a white sign and true reds, but its crop leaves out the tomatoes, the first item the client named, and it barely removes the grain (noise only drops from 2.95 to 2.41, so it fails the denoise check). A keeps all three products and the sign in the frame and cleans the grain well without turning it to mush. Its weakness is a leftover green-cream cast on the sign and a slightly faded, film-like tone, but the crop and noise rank higher on the brief, so A is the one the client could still use.

A's crop drops the tomatoes completely, and Rosa named them as one of the three things in her photo. B keeps the tomatoes, jalapeños, plums and price sign together in a balanced frame. A has the more accurate white balance, but it still shows obvious grain and fails the denoise check. B's clean, detailed denoise and complete subject outweigh its leftover greenish-yellow cast on the sign.

B brings back the dusk sky the client asked for: blue above, warm orange-gold toward the horizon. Its white balance and exposure are close to the reference, and the barn walls stay white. A loses the orange glow and turns the sky a muddy purple-grey with a greenish band near the horizon; it is underexposed overall and fails the exposure and white-balance checks. Both are still slightly tilted and B's sky gradient is a little heavy-handed, but A's colour cast is the bigger fault for a Christmas card.

A keeps the brief's warm orange dusk glow at the horizon under a deeper blue sky, with exposure and white balance close to the reference. B's sky has turned an unnatural purple with a greenish band where the orange glow should be, and the whole image is about a stop too dark (exposure and white balance both fail). Neither is fully level, but A is closer (1.05° vs 1.55°). A's slightly heavy sharpening and a visible step in the sky gradient are smaller faults than B's colour cast.

B reads as one coherent scene: the path winds up and actually reaches the small church, the layered hills give real depth, and the top quarter is left as calm, empty dark sky. A has serious construction faults. Its church floats in the sky above the hills with a skewed base, the path breaks into a detached pointed sliver, and the lantern and arc strokes look pasted on. A's moon also sits partly inside the top quarter that was meant to stay clear. B has its own small flaws: a stray roof sliver, snow caps sitting slightly off the trees, and a weak sense of glowing light. Even so, its composition and shapes are much more deliberate and would hold up at thumbnail size.

A leaves the top quarter completely calm for the title. Its path leads the eye straight to the house, and the layered hills read clearly even as a thumbnail, though its warm light is understated and it has small flaws: a stray sliver beside the roof and snow caps that sit oddly on the trees. B puts a large moon inside the top quarter where the client will set 'Advent'. Its craft also breaks down: the house floats in the sky on a slanted base, the path ends in a point in mid-air, and the lantern and grey arcs look like floating filler.

B is closer to the brief: its stand body is red under a green roof, while A's is mostly green with only a red awning strip. B also has a bolder silhouette, with a thick outline, an arched roof and a solid dark display panel, so it holds together better as a thumbnail. A's produce is bigger and easier to read, but its overlapping corn and honey pot, the floating side sprigs and the extra shades of red and green make it busier and less controlled. B's main weakness is its tiny produce, especially the unclear corn ear, which will mostly disappear at 64 px.

A matches the brief more closely: it shows a red stand under a green roof, uses a tight palette with one dark-green outline, and the tomato, corn and honey jar sit cleanly in a dark window, so the silhouette still reads at thumbnail size. B's stand is mostly green line-work rather than red, the produce cluster is muddy (the corn looks like bread loaves, the honey pot is unclear), and the matching leaf sprigs on each side look like floating clip-art filler. B also adds darker shades of red and gold beyond the four-color limit, while A's slips are smaller and its shapes feel more deliberate and handmade.

B's grilled cheese reads clearly as a toasted triangle resting beside the bowl, and its wobbly hand-drawn outlines and slightly tilted window feel genuinely hand-made. A's sandwich looks like a stiff upright plaque, and its flat vector shapes (lamp, napkin) look closer to clip-art. B has flaws: stray table-grain lines cut across the bowl and its grey-teal wall is less warm than A's beige room, but its subject reads better and its focal point is stronger at thumbnail size.

B is the warmer, cozier picture the brief asked for: a lamp-lit cream wall, a clean, well-layered soup bowl with a basil garnish, and a clear value step from the light wall down to the dark table. A's grilled cheese reads better as a sandwich, but its palette is a cold, murky grey-green, and dark lines cut across the soup bowl, which looks like a mistake. B has its own problems (the upright toast slice reads more like bread than grilled cheese, and the napkin looks pasted on), but these are smaller than A's cold mood and visible errors.

B passes all 10 checks. A fails the decay check: it ends at -23 dB, so its last note is cut short by an 18 ms fade instead of ringing out. B is also the better-designed chime, with layered, slightly inharmonic bell partials that give it a bright, clean character, while A uses a plain sine plus one second harmonic. B's flaw is that each note's buffer is cut off at about 15% amplitude, and the faint vertical lines at those points in its spectrogram mean audible clicks; A's per-note release tapers avoid this, which keeps the margin slight.

A passes all 10 checks and decays cleanly to -48.5 dB, while B fails the decay check, ending at only -23.3 dB, so its final note sounds clipped short rather than ringing out. A builds each note from slightly inharmonic, bell-like partials into a bright rising G-B-D triad, whereas B is close to plain sines with one soft second harmonic. A's one flaw is that each note is cut off at 0.48 s while still at about 15% amplitude, which shows as faint vertical lines in its spectrogram.

Both pass all 9 checks with similar length and peak, and both spectrograms show a clean broadband burst with no clicks or hum lines. A sounds more like real paper: its noise is spectrally shaped with random flutter, it has six small decaying crease grains, and the last ones form a soft settle. B's band-limited noise looks boxy in the spectrogram, with hard upper and lower edges, and its 13.7/21.3 Hz sine flutter risks an audible regular pulse. B's settle is a single faint noise tail.

Both scripts pass all 9 checks with similar length and peak, so the choice comes down to design. B's sound is a swell-and-decay noise bed with random, non-rhythmic flutter, small crease grains and a quiet settle at the end. That reads more like real paper than A's even plateau, which has periodic 13.7/21.3 Hz flutter and hard, stepped band edges in the spectrogram. B's weaknesses are energy extending below 100 Hz and a brighter, hissier centroid (8.9 kHz), but it still has more natural variation and detail.

Each script fails one check. A comes in 2 dB too loud (-22 LUFS), a fault but one that a simple gain change fixes. B fails the droplet check (CV 0.22 against 0.43, with higher flatness), so it leans toward the plain static the brief warned against. A's spectrogram shows separate bright drop flecks scattered across about 800 Hz to 4 kHz over an even wash. B's flecks bunch into a narrow 1.3–2 kHz strip that reads more like a band than individual drops on metal, and B hits its loudness through a hardcoded gain guess rather than measuring it as A does.

A hits the brief's hard delivery spec, landing exactly at -24 LUFS with a safe true peak. B lands at -22 LUFS, outside the ±1.5 window, a loudness fault the rubric names explicitly; its ffmpeg calibration pass also makes it less robust offline. B does have the more convincing drops: its pings are scattered across 0.8–4 kHz and it passes the droplet check, while A's drops sit in a narrow 1.2–1.8 kHz strip over a bright, static-like wash and fail it. A still edges ahead because it meets the hard spec and is built for looping, with a crossfaded seam, drops that wrap across the loop point, and a stereo wash.

Both meet every hard requirement. A lands exactly on -23 LUFS and has more peak headroom. A moves through G, D/F#, Em7 and Cadd9, then returns to G. Its pulse stops at 27.5 s so the last chord can ring out, giving the reverent ending a clear resolution. B ends on a D-major pad, so the cue is left unresolved, and its four-note G-B-D-B pluck repeats unchanged for the whole 30 s, while A changes its pulse notes and adds soft high notes at the phrase boundaries.

Both pass every hard check, so the choice comes down to musical shape. B moves through five chords (G, D/F#, Em7, Cadd9, back to G), so the harmony returns home and the final G chord fades out over its last stretch. A's pad finishes on an unresolved D major, with only a single low G pluck to suggest a cadence. B also has more going on in the arrangement: accented downbeats that switch between mallet and pluck, a pulse line that moves, and quiet upper notes at the phrase boundaries. A is the smoother bed, with crossfaded pads and a longer 1.8 s fade, while B dips briefly in loudness between chords.

A fails two hard requirements: its true peak measures +2.0 dBTP and it has 464 clipped samples, because it applies a fixed gain boost and then hard-clips. Its key also reads as F# minor rather than the A major asked for. B meets every measured requirement (-16.0 LUFS, -2.8 dBTP, 30.0 s, A major) and has the same layered groove of drums, bass, offbeat chord plucks and a varied mallet motif. It also ends with a deliberate E-to-A cadence that rings out.

A passes all nine checks. B has a true peak of +2.0 dBTP and 464 clipped samples, because it applied a +5.5 dB gain on top of normalization and then hard-clipped, so it fails the brief's peak limit outright. Musically the two are close: both loop A–D–F#m–E over a steady 124 BPM groove with a plucked hook and end on a ringing A chord. A also has a cleaner arrangement, with a motif that holds back until after the intro and an E-to-A cadence before its decaying final chord.

B hits the requested 80 BPM and reads as A minor. A measures 113.5 BPM, and its chromagram is dominated by a constant E, so it was estimated as E minor, which suggests a held drone. B's pictures show real musical motion: plucked chords changing every 1.5 s through a progression, a returning E-G-A-G motif, and a soft pulse that holds. A is a thick sustained pad that barely moves. B's weaknesses are that its harmony thins to bare bass pulses after about 15 s and it ends with 1.9 s of near-silence (its failed check). That costs less than A's missed tempo and static, drone-like texture.

A hits the asked 80 BPM and reads as A minor. Its chromagram shows chords moving every 1.5 s, a recurring E-G-A motif and a steady soft pulse, so it has real harmonic motion, though the harmony thins out after about 15 s, which caused its dead-air flag. B fails the tempo check (measured 113.5 BPM) and is detected in E minor because a held E dominates throughout. Its spectrogram is one dense, static mono pad with constant high bands, so it has much less movement and pulse than A.

Both videos show exactly the seven required lines and nothing extra. B reveals them in the order the brief asks for (what, when, where, price), with each card easing in at a readable pace. A shows almost everything in the first 4.7 seconds and then sits nearly frozen for 10 seconds (static fraction 0.89). B also reads better on a phone: a bold red firehouse banner, cream cards and a red price block give a clear hierarchy and a warm, local feel. A has a small department name, a large empty dark gap in the middle and small type at the bottom, though B's lower half stays sparse for the first few seconds.

Both videos show exactly the seven required lines with no extra text, so the decision comes down to design and motion. A brings in what, when, where and price one at a time as eased cards under a strong red department banner, which matches the requested order. B shows the event name, date and time at about 0.15s, then location and price at about 4.1s, and then holds still for roughly ten seconds (static fraction 0.89). B also sets the department name in tiny 29px type and leaves a large empty gap in the middle. A's price card arrives late and its lower half stays empty for a long time, but its order and hierarchy are much easier to read on a phone.

Both videos show the three KJV lines and 'Psalm 46:10' spelled correctly with nothing extra, so the text is even. A brings the lines in one by one about 1.6–1.7 s apart, each fading in with a small eased drift, and the reference lands at about 5 s, a prayerful pace. B fades all three lines in within about 1.5 s, and its frames barely change for most of the clip, which fails the not-static check (0.73 static). B's thin inset frame and readable italic reference look more deliberate than A's plain stack. But A's larger 65 px type reads better on a phone, and its pacing makes it the better post, despite A's tiny, faint reference and its oddly smaller middle line.

Both cards show exactly the three KJV lines and 'Psalm 46:10' with nothing invented, and both use a centred serif stack on dark teal. B brings the lines in at a calm, readable pace over about six seconds, with a small eased upward drift, a moving light shift, and larger 65px type that reads better on a phone. A fades everything in within about 3.6 seconds using small 52px type, then sits nearly frozen and fails the not-static check. B's smaller middle line and tiny, faint reference are weaker choices, but they matter less than A's rushed start and long freeze.

Both videos show exactly the six requested lines with no invented figures, and both use simple cuts with eased count-ups and progress bars. B ends on a summary slate with all four results in labelled rows under the title and year, which suits an annual meeting better than A ending on the 38% card alone for about four seconds. A's cream-on-dark-teal cards have bigger, more contrasty numerals, but B's warm paper-and-green palette has more point of view, even though each of its stats holds for only about 1.3 seconds before the next one appears.

Both videos show every line spelled correctly, with no invented numbers or dates, and every count settles on the exact figure. B is the better design: big cream numbers on a dark forest-green panel with a gold accent for the farms figure, which reads better on a phone than A's mid-green on cream and its small type on the summary card.
